name: 16:8 time-restricted eating

lead: 16:8 time-restricted eating means eating all meals within eight hours and fasting for the other sixteen. People use it to lose body fat and get a leaner face and body, with a simple daily structure.

The window tends to reduce total calorie intake, and fat loss is what shows up in the mirror. Trials, mostly small and lasting weeks to months in overweight adults, athletes and lifters, have measured weight and metabolic markers, and reviews report weight loss broadly similar to ordinary calorie restriction.

paras: Most people skip breakfast or stop eating early in the evening, fasting overnight plus part of the morning or evening. Black coffee, tea and water are typically allowed in the fasting hours. Lifters often keep protein high inside the window. Changes in body fat accumulate over weeks to months.

Reported short-term effects include hunger, irritability, headaches and poor concentration. Reviews advise against it in pregnancy, for young people, underweight people and anyone with an eating-disorder history.

angle.text: Users adopt a daily eight-hour eating window as an easy way to eat less and lose fat, which shows as a sharper face and leaner body. Trials have measured weight and metabolic markers, so the look comes through the fat-loss pathway.

lead: 16:8 time-restricted eating (TRE) is a daily meal-timing pattern in which all food is eaten within an eight-hour window, leaving sixteen hours of fasting that usually span the night plus part of the morning or evening. It is one variant of time-restricted eating, in which food is confined to a set daily window, commonly 8 to 12 hours.[1]

In looksmaxxing and wider fitness culture it is used mainly for leanness. Followers adopt it to lower body fat, to look more defined in the face and midsection, and to simplify eating routines by cutting the number of meals to plan. Some lifters pair it with a calorie surplus, using the window to fit large meals while still training hard.[2][3][4]

Published trials have studied the pattern in overweight adults, endurance runners and cyclists, dancers and resistance-trained lifters, generally in small groups over weeks to months.[5][2][6][7][8] Reviews describe the wider evidence on intermittent fasting as preliminary, with long-term effects not well studied and an advantage over ordinary calorie restriction that is limited.[1]

paras: Intermittent fasting is an umbrella term for schedules that alternate periods of fasting or markedly reduced intake with normal eating. Its main forms are alternate-day fasting, periodic fasting such as the 5:2 diet, and daily time-restricted eating.[1] Time-restricted eating differs from the other two in that it does not change which days are fasted but limits the hours of each day in which food is eaten. The 16:8 version is the best-known; stricter variants compress eating into one to two hours, as in one-meal-a-day plans.[1]

Some versions align the window with daylight hours, for example from after sunrise to around sunset, while others let the person choose a window that fits their schedule. A trial in middle-aged cyclists used a self-selected 16:8 window rather than a fixed clock time.[6][7] During the fast, practitioners typically allow water and unsweetened drinks such as coffee or tea; protocols differ on this and trials generally specify their own rules.

In fitness circles the pattern is often associated with the Leangains approach, a lifting-oriented version that popularised eating within a shortened daily window around training. Forum discussion treats 16:8 as the entry-level version of the idea and longer fasts as progressions from it.

Therapeutic fasting for obesity was studied as early as 1915, and interest revived in the 1960s after an enthusiastic report by Bloom and colleagues; early fasts lasted from one to fourteen days.[1] The 5:2 diet appeared in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie and Mark Mattson, and Michael Mosley popularised it in the United Kingdom and Australia in 2012 through the BBC documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer.[1]

Daily time-restricted eating gained a research profile through studies of circadian biology, which found that glucose metabolism and the hormone leptin follow a daily rhythm. Preliminary work has linked eating during the hours of melatonin secretion with higher glucose in young healthy adults.[1] Researchers describe meal timing as a potential new target for weight control, while stressing that the evidence is early.[1]

Intermittent fasting became a prominent diet trend in the late 2010s; a 2018 survey by the International Food Information Council ranked it the most popular diet that year, and it spread through Silicon Valley, celebrity endorsements and fitness media.[1] T Nation published articles on time-restricted feeding plans, including a 2016 piece titled The Time-Restricted-Plus Diet that discussed an eating window as a way to get and stay lean.[3][4]

The most direct route to fat loss is energy intake: with fewer hours available, many people eat fewer calories, although trials differ in whether participants were asked to count calories. In the seven-week Orthodox fasting comparison, the TRE arm followed a low-calorie 16/8 pattern, so intake restriction and timing were combined.[9]

Reviews describe additional proposed mechanisms. One is a metabolic switch: as fasting continues past the fed state (about four hours) and post-absorptive state, the body moves toward mobilising fat and using ketones, a transition described at roughly 12 to 36 hours of fasting, which a 16-hour fast may only partly reach.[1] Another is circadian alignment of food intake with the body's daily rhythm.[1] Studies of hormones such as irisin, nesfatin and lipolytic hormones in 16:8 groups explore these pathways.[8][10][11]

Reviews of intermittent fasting generally report weight loss of roughly 2.5 to 9.9 percent in adults with overweight or obesity, mostly fat mass with some lean-mass loss; for time-restricted eating, one summary reports a fat-to-lean loss ratio of about 4:1.[1] Cardiometabolic changes such as lower waist circumference, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting insulin are described as broadly similar to those seen with continuous calorie restriction, and the effect on blood pressure is smaller.[1]

Evidence that intermittent fasting outperforms ordinary calorie restriction for weight loss is described as limited.[1] A 2019 review cited dropout rates of 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[1]

Reviews also note that fasting before prolonged exercise lasting over 60 minutes reduces performance and that intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance in general.[1] Practitioners who train fasted or schedule workouts inside the window describe it differently, reporting that it suits their routines.[3][4]

Runners: an 8-week randomized trial in 23 male middle- and long-distance runners assigned 12 to 16:8 TRE and 11 to habitual eating while both continued habitual training. It measured body composition, energy and macronutrient intake, indices of endurance performance and metabolic health markers.[5]

Resistance-trained participants: 17 well-trained men (10) and women (7) were randomized to hypercaloric 16:8 TRE or a control pattern during supervised progressive resistance exercise four times a week. Both groups ate a 10 percent calorie surplus with 2.2 g per kg of daily protein, so the trial tested whether a restricted window affects muscle mass and strength under surplus conditions.[2]

Cyclists: studies in middle-aged male cyclists examined a self-selected 16:8 protocol and reported effects on fat oxidation, cardiometabolic markers and 10-km cycling performance in one report and cardiovascular markers in a quasi-experimental follow-up.[6][7]
Dancers: a study of female DanceSport dancers examined body composition and lipolytic hormones under 16/8 TRE.[8]

Overweight adults: in a study comparing a 7-week Orthodox religious fasting pattern (29 overweight adults) with a low-calorie 16/8 pattern (16 matched adults), both groups showed a trend toward weight loss at week 7 and measures were taken again six weeks after the diets ended.[9] Companion analyses from the same research program examined plasma irisin concentrations and nesfatin-related beta-cell function.[10][11]

Oral health: a three-arm trial of 66 healthy participants compared Bahai dry fasting, 16:8 TRE and a regular diet during experimentally induced gingivitis; the dry-fasting arm showed a smaller rise in gum bleeding than the other two arms.[12]

A 12-month randomized trial in adults with obesity compared a ketogenic diet with intermittent fasting on metabolic and orexin-A responses, and a real-world observational study in Chinese office workers tracked short-term BMI changes with self-selected diet patterns.[13][14]

Short-term effects reported for intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired concentration, usually fading within about a month.[1] A 2018 systematic review found no major adverse effects, though reviews note that adverse effects have not been comprehensively studied.[1]

Health authorities and reviews advise against these diets for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people and people with or prone to eating disorders.[1] The US National Institute on Aging calls the research limited and inconclusive, the American Heart Association reports no good evidence of heart benefit, and the New Zealand Ministry of Health advises against it for people with diabetes.[1]

The pattern is discussed as a way to stay lean and reduce facial puffiness, often alongside calorie counting and lifting. Posters on T Nation describe the eating window as an easy-to-follow structure; the site's articles characterise modest time-restricted plans as working as well as stricter ones.[3][4] Published studies of facial appearance under TRE were not located; reported outcomes concern body composition and metabolic markers.

lore.intro: On lifting and fat-loss forums such as T Nation, 16:8 and related windows are discussed as simple tools for getting lean without elaborate meal planning.[3][4]

claims.claim: An eating window is an easy way to get lean.
Fasting preserves muscle while cutting fat.
A shorter window reduces facial puffiness.
Longer or stricter windows work better than 16:8.

timeline.event: Therapeutic fasting for obesity is studied in medical literature.[1]
Interest in fasting for obesity revives after a report by Bloom and colleagues.[1]
The 5:2 diet is first documented in an article co-authored by Michelle Harvie and Mark Mattson.[1]
BBC Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer popularises intermittent fasting in the UK and Australia.[1]
T Nation publishes The Time-Restricted-Plus Diet, discussing eating-window plans for leanness.[3]
An International Food Information Council survey ranks intermittent fasting the most popular diet of the year.[1]
Randomized trial of 8 weeks of 16:8 TRE in male runners is published.[5]
Trial of hypercaloric 16:8 TRE during resistance training is published.[2]
